title: 〜を (object)
meaning: Comes after a noun and marks the direct object of a transitive verb: the person or thing the action acts on.

senses.label: Object of an action
senses.meaning: Marks the person or thing directly affected by the action, like the object after an English verb. But Japanese word order is “object + を + verb”: the verb comes last. 「を」 is pronounced “o”.
senses.connection: Noun + を + 食べる／飲む／見る／読む／書く／買う and other transitive verbs
examples: I eat bread every morning.
Yesterday I bought a magazine at the bookstore.
I watch TV every evening.

senses.label: 「〜をする」
senses.meaning: An activity noun before 「する」 is marked with 「を」. It means “do (an activity)”. You can use it for sports, study, work, housework and more.
senses.connection: Noun + を + する (テニスをする／宿題をする／料理をする)
examples: On weekends I play tennis with friends.
Did you do your homework?
On Sunday I cleaned my room.

notes: The objects of 「好き」, 「わかる」, 「できる」, 「ほしい」 and 「上手」 take 「が」, not 「を」: ✕「日本語をわかります」→ ○「日本語がわかります」.
The person you meet with 「会う」 and the vehicle you get on with 「乗る」 take 「に」, not 「を」: ✕「友達を会う」→ ○「友達に会う」; ✕「電車を乗る」→ ○「電車に乗る」.
Don't use 「を」 before an intransitive verb. Use 「が」 instead, or switch to the matching transitive verb: ✕「ドアを閉まる」→ ○「ドアを閉める」 (transitive) / ○「ドアが閉まる」 (intransitive).
One verb can take only one 「を」: ✕「日本語を勉強をする」→ ○「日本語を勉強する」 or 「日本語の勉強をする」.
The particle 「を」 is pronounced “o”, but it must always be written 「を」, never 「お」: ✕「パンお食べます」.

etymology: One theory says 「を」 was originally an interjection-like particle used for emotion or emphasis, and later became fixed as the case particle for objects. It was pronounced “wo” in old Japanese and “o” today. Under modern kana rules, only this particle keeps the spelling 「を」.

similar.title: 〜を (route / departure)
similar.explanation: The same particle 「を」 (same origin). In this use it comes before a transitive verb and marks what the action acts on. The route/departure 「を」 comes before movement verbs like 「歩く」, 「渡る」 or 「出る」 and marks the path you take or the place you leave: 「道を歩く」, 「家を出る」.

similar.title: 〜をください
similar.explanation: A set phrase built on this use (same origin): 「を」 marks the thing you want, and 「ください」 turns it into a request. Used when shopping or ordering: 「水をください」.

similar.title: 〜が好き・〜が嫌い・〜が上手・〜が下手
similar.explanation: In English “like” and “be good at” take a direct object, so learners often compare them with 「を」. But 「好き」 and 「上手」 are adjectives, so the thing liked takes 「が」: 「音楽が好きです」, not 「音楽を好きです」 (heard occasionally in speech, but not standard).

similar.title: 〜がわかる・〜ができる
similar.explanation: In English you “understand Japanese” or “can swim” with a direct object, but 「わかる」 and 「できる」 express ability or a state, so their object takes 「が」: 「日本語がわかります」, 「テニスができます」. This contrasts neatly with the rule “the object of an action takes を”.

formation: 「を」 is a single case particle and can't be broken down further. The pattern is simply “noun + を + transitive verb”. 「を」 marks the noun in front of it as the thing the action directly acts on, and the verb goes at the end of the sentence. Because roles are shown by particles rather than word order, the object can even move in front of the subject without changing the meaning, as long as it keeps its 「を」: 「パンを私が食べた」. In 「〜をする」, an activity noun is treated as the object of 「する」, so “doing an activity” also uses 「を」. And since 「を」 marks “the object of this one action”, a single verb is generally considered unable to take two 「を」.

title: 〜を (route / departure)
meaning: Used with movement verbs. It marks the place you move through, or the place you leave.
connection: Place noun + を + movement verb (歩く・渡る・出る・降りる etc.)

senses.label: Place passed through
senses.meaning: Shows that you move through, across or along a place: “walk along”, “go through”, “cross”. Common verbs are 「歩く」, 「走る」, 「渡る」, 「通る」, 「散歩する」, 「曲がる」 and 「飛ぶ」.
senses.connection: Place + を + 歩く／走る／渡る／通る／散歩する／曲がる／飛ぶ
examples: I take a walk in the park every morning.
Please cross this bridge.
Turn right at the next corner.

senses.label: Starting point you leave
senses.meaning: Shows the place you leave or get out of: “leave”, “get out of”, “get off”. Common verbs are 「出る」, 「降りる」, 「出発する」 and 「卒業する」.
senses.connection: Place + を + 出る／降りる／出発する／卒業する／離れる
examples: I leave home at seven every morning.
I get off the train at the next station.
My older brother graduated from university last year.

notes: 「大学を出る」 usually means “to graduate from university”; to say “walk out of the campus” you use 「大学から出る」. Changing the particle changes the meaning.
Getting on takes 「に」 and getting off takes 「を」. Mix them up and the sentence is wrong: ✕「電車を乗る」→ ○「電車に乗る」; ✕「電車に降りる」→ ○「電車を降りる」.
Moving through or along a place takes 「を」, not 「で」: ✕「横断歩道で渡る」→ ○「横断歩道を渡る」.
「歩く」 and 「出る」 are intransitive verbs, but they still take 「を」 for the route or the place you leave. Don't switch to 「が」 just because the verb is intransitive: ✕「公園が散歩する」→ ○「公園を散歩する」.

etymology: This is the same particle as the object 「を」. In old Japanese, 「を」 could already mark the place you move through and the place you leave, and this use has survived to the present day.

similar.title: 〜を (object)
similar.explanation: The same particle 「を」 (same origin). The object 「を」 comes before a transitive verb and marks what the action acts on (「パンを食べる」); this use comes before a movement verb and marks the route you take or the place you leave (「橋を渡る」, 「部屋を出る」).

similar.title: 〜から (starting point)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning when talking about leaving. 「から」 highlights the starting point, “out from inside”, and works with any action (in 「家から駅まで歩く」 you can't use 「を」). 「を」 only goes with leaving verbs like 「出る」, 「降りる」 or 「離れる」 and expresses leaving in general. Both 「部屋から出る」 and 「部屋を出る」 are fine, but 「大学を出る」 usually means graduating.

similar.title: 〜で (place of action)
similar.explanation: Both are about places, so they're often compared. 「で」 only marks the area where an action happens (「川で泳ぐ」: swim in the river); 「を」 marks a place you move through or along (「川を泳いで渡る」: swim across the river).

formation: This 「を」 is the same particle as the object 「を」. It marks “what the action covers or deals with”. With a movement verb, what is “covered” is a stretch of space: in 「道を歩く」, the whole road is the route you move along; in 「家を出る」, the house is the starting point you leave. That's why 「を」 is used even though 「歩く」 and 「出る」 are intransitive: here 「を」 doesn't mark something that is affected, but the space that the movement passes through or leaves. Compared with 「で」, which only says where an action takes place, 「を」 makes the place part of the movement itself. That is the difference between 「道を歩く」 (walk along the road) and 「道で遊ぶ」 (play on the road).

title: 〜に (point in time)
meaning: Comes after a noun for a specific time and shows when an action happens, like “at”, “on” or “in” in English.
connection: Specific time noun + に (〜時に／〜日に／〜曜日に／〜年に)

senses.label: Clock time, date, day of the week
senses.meaning: Shows the specific point in time when something happens. Times, dates and years with numbers, and days of the week, usually take 「に」. Like “at six”, “on the 5th”, “in 2020”.
senses.connection: Number + 時／分／日／月／年 + に; 〜曜日 + に
examples: I get up at six every morning.
On Sunday I went to see a movie.
I came to Japan in 2020.

senses.label: Holidays and special periods
senses.meaning: Shows that you do something on a holiday, in a season or during a certain period. With words like 「春」 or 「夏休み」, 「に」 is optional; adding it stresses the time.
senses.connection: 誕生日／クリスマス／夏休み／週末 etc. + に
examples: I got a watch for my birthday.
I'm going to Hokkaido during summer vacation.
I clean my room on the weekend.

notes: Relative time words such as 「今日」, 「明日」, 「昨日」, 「毎日」, 「今」, 「来週」 and 「去年」 don't take 「に」: ✕「明日に行きます」→ ○「明日行きます」.

「まで」 and 「までに」 mean completely different things: 「五時まで待ちます」 means “I'll wait until five”; 「五時までに来てください」 means “Please come by five”. Mixing them up can cause real misunderstandings about times and deadlines.
Don't use 「で」 for an appointed time: ✕「三時で会いましょう」→ ○「三時に会いましょう」. In 「三時で終わります」, 「で」 marks a cut-off point, not a point in time.
Words like 「朝」, 「夜」 and 「夏」 usually don't take 「に」; adding it sounds as if you're stressing them. Specific points in time like 「〜曜日」, 「〜月〜日」 and 「〜時」 usually do take 「に」.

etymology: 「に」 is a very old case particle. Its basic job is to mark the “point” where an action is located or arrives. Points in time and points in space use the same 「に」. One theory says the copula 「なり」 came from 「に＋あり」.

similar.title: 〜ごろ
similar.explanation: Both express time and are close in meaning: 「三時に」 is exactly “at three”; 「三時ごろ」 is roughly “around three”. You can use them together: 「三時ごろ（に）来てください」.

similar.title: 〜までに
similar.explanation: Both involve a point in time and are often compared: 「五時に帰る」 means going home at five o'clock; 「五時までに帰る」 means going home any time before five (a deadline).

similar.title: 〜に (place of existence)
similar.explanation: The same particle 「に」 (same origin). Both mark a “point”: a point in time (「七時に起きる」) and a point in space where something exists (「部屋にいる」) use the same 「に」.

formation: The core meaning of 「に」 is “the one point where an action lands”. After a time or date, it treats that time as a point on the timeline, and the action happens at that point. So only absolute times that can be fixed on the timeline (「三時」, 「五月五日」, 「日曜日」) take 「に」. Relative words like 「今日」 and 「明日」, which are measured from the moment of speaking, already work like adverbs and modify the verb directly, so they don't take 「に」. 「〜ごろ」 expresses a range rather than an exact point, so 「に」 is optional after it.

title: 〜に (place of existence)
meaning: Comes after a place noun and shows where a person or thing is. It often goes with verbs of existence or staying, like 「ある」, 「いる」 and 「住む」.
connection: Place noun + に + ある／いる／住む etc.

senses.label: Where someone or something is
senses.meaning: Shows that a person or thing exists somewhere. The common pattern is 「place に + thing が + ある」 or 「place に + person が + いる」, like “There is ... in/on ...”. Use 「ある」 for non-living things and 「いる」 for people and animals.
senses.connection: Place + に + noun + が + あります／います
examples: There is a book on the desk.
There is a cat in the yard.
There is a big supermarket near the station.

senses.label: Living and staying
senses.meaning: With verbs like 「住む」, 「泊まる」, 「勤める」 and 「座る」, it shows where you stay, for a long time or a short time: “live in”, “stay at”, “sit on”.
senses.connection: Place + に + 住む／泊まる／勤める／座る／置く
examples: I live in Tokyo.
Tonight I'm staying at a hotel.
Please have a seat in this chair.

notes: The place where an action happens takes 「で」, not 「に」: ✕「図書館に勉強します」→ ○「図書館で勉強します」. Use 「に」 only for existing or staying somewhere.
「住む」 and 「勤める」 take 「に」, but 「暮らす」 and 「働く」 take 「で」: ✕「東京で住んでいます」→ ○「東京に住んでいます」 / ○「東京で暮らしています」.
Use 「いる」 for people and animals, 「ある」 for things: ✕「先生があります」→ ○「先生がいます」. Using 「ある」 for a person is a common mistake and sounds as if you're treating them like an object.
When asking where your boss or a client is, use honorific language: 「田中様は今どちらにいらっしゃいますか」. Asking 「どこにいますか」 directly sounds rude.

etymology: This is the same case particle as 「に」 for time. Its basic meaning is the “point” where something exists or arrives. In old Japanese, 「に」 also marked the place before 「あり」 (“to be, to exist”).

similar.title: 〜は〜にある・〜は〜にいる (location)
similar.explanation: Also uses 「に」 for location and is close in meaning; only the focus differs. 「場所に物がある」 says “there is something in a place”; 「物は場所にある」 says “where something is”. Use the second when asking the way: 「トイレはどこにありますか」.

similar.title: 〜がある・〜がいる (existence)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning and often used together. This entry focuses on the place of existence marked by 「に」; 「がある／がいる」 focuses on what exists and on the difference between 「ある」 (things) and 「いる」 (people and animals).

similar.title: 〜で (place of action)
similar.explanation: Both mark places and are the easiest to confuse. 「に」 marks where something statically exists (「教室に学生がいる」); 「で」 marks where an action happens (「教室で勉強する」).

similar.title: 〜に (point in time)
similar.explanation: The same particle 「に」 (same origin). The core meaning of both is a “point”: a point in space where something exists, and a point in time.

formation: The pattern is “place noun + に + existence verb (ある／いる／住む, etc.)”. The core meaning of 「に」 is “the point something settles on or attaches to”. Existence verbs describe something “staying” in a place, so 「に」 marks the place as the point that state is attached to. There is no process of action here, only the state of “being there”, so Japanese uses 「に」, the particle of a “point”, rather than 「で」, which marks the stage where an action takes place. 「住む」 and 「勤める」 also describe “settling” somewhere, so they take 「に」 too.

title: 〜に (destination / target)
meaning: Marks the destination or arrival point of movement, and the person an action is directed at.
connection: Place noun + に + movement verb; person + に + verb

senses.label: Destination
senses.meaning: Marks where you are going or arriving: “go to”, “come to”, “return to”, “arrive at”. Often used with 「行く」, 「来る」, 「帰る」 and 「着く」.
senses.connection: Place + に + 行く／来る／帰る／着く
examples: I'm going to the bank tomorrow.
I go home at six every day.
The plane arrived at the airport at ten.

senses.label: Place you enter or get on
senses.meaning: Marks the place you go into, get on or go up into: “enter”, “get on”. Often used with 「入る」, 「乗る」 and 「上がる」.
senses.connection: Place／vehicle + に + 入る／乗る／上がる
examples: I take a bath every evening.
I got on the bus at the station.
Please come into the room.

senses.label: Person the action is aimed at
senses.meaning: Marks the person an action is directed at: “to”, “for”, “with”. Often used with 「あげる」, 「電話する」, 「会う」, 「聞く」, 「教える」 and 「手紙を書く」.
senses.connection: Person + に + あげる／電話する／会う／聞く／教える／書く
examples: I gave a present to my friend.
Yesterday I called my mother.
I ran into my teacher at the station.

notes: With giving and receiving verbs, the direction of 「に」 can flip: 「友達に本をあげる」 means giving a book to a friend; 「友達に本をもらう」 means getting a book from a friend. Look at the verb to work out the direction; get it wrong and the meaning is reversed.
The person you meet with 「会う」 takes 「に」 or 「と」, not 「を」: ✕「先生を会う」→ ○「先生に会う」.
Getting on takes 「に」 and getting off takes 「を」: ✕「バスを乗る」→ ○「バスに乗る」; ✕「バスに降りる」→ ○「バスを降りる」.
Don't say 「先生に〜てあげます」 to a superior or someone older: it sounds as if you're doing them a favor, which is quite rude. Use 「お〜します」, or leave out the giving/receiving verb: 「先生に資料をお送りします」.

etymology: This 「に」 shares its origin with the other uses of 「に」. Its basic meaning is “the point where an action lands”. A destination in space and a person who receives something are both the final “point” the action reaches.

similar.title: 〜へ (direction)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning when marking a destination, and mostly interchangeable: 「学校に行く」, 「学校へ行く」. 「に」 focuses on the point of arrival and can also mark the person an action is directed at; 「へ」 focuses on the direction of movement.

similar.title: 〜に行く・〜に来る (purpose)
similar.explanation: The same 「に」 (same origin), both pointing to “where you're heading”. In 「図書館に行く」, 「に」 follows a place and marks the destination; in 「本を借りに行く」, 「に」 follows a verb's ます-stem and marks the purpose of going.

similar.title: 〜と (and / with)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning when the other party is a person: 「友達に会う」 can mean going to see someone one-sidedly or bumping into them; 「友達と会う」 stresses that both people arranged to meet.

similar.title: 〜に〜をあげる・くれる・もらう (giving and receiving things)
similar.explanation: The same 「に」 used in giving and receiving (same origin): with 「あげる」 and 「くれる」, 「に」 marks the receiver; with 「もらう」, 「に」 marks the giver (and can be replaced with 「から」).

formation: The core meaning of 「に」 is “the point an action finally reaches or settles on”. With movement verbs, that point is the place you arrive at (「駅に着く」). With 「入る」, 「乗る」 or 「座る」, it's the place you enter or attach to (「部屋に入る」). With 「書く」, 「電話する」 or 「あげる」, it's the person the action or the thing finally reaches (「友達に手紙を書く」 = the letter reaches the friend). 「もらう」 and 「借りる」 also use 「に」; here it marks the other end of the exchange, which is why it can be replaced with 「から」. Once you grasp the core idea of an “arrival point”, it's clear why 「に」 can follow both places and people.

title: 〜で (place of action)
meaning: Comes after a place noun and shows where an action happens, like “at” or “in” in English.

senses.label: Place of an action
senses.meaning: Shows where an action takes place: “do ... at/in ...”. It comes before action verbs like 「勉強する」, 「食べる」, 「遊ぶ」, 「働く」 and 「買う」.
senses.connection: Place + で + 勉強する／食べる／遊ぶ／働く／買う／待つ
examples: I study at the library every day.
Yesterday I bought shoes at a department store.
Please wait here for a moment.

senses.label: Place of an event
senses.meaning: Shows where an activity, event or party is held, or where something happens. 「ある」 is used here, but it means “take place”, so the place takes 「で」, not 「に」.
senses.connection: Place + で + noun (パーティー／試験／事故 etc.) + が + ある
examples: There's an exam at school tomorrow.
There's a party at a friend's house on Saturday.
There was an accident in front of the station.

notes: Existence takes 「に」, actions take 「で」: ✕「部屋で猫がいる」→ ○「部屋に猫がいる」; ✕「公園に遊ぶ」→ ○「公園で遊ぶ」.
「住む」 takes 「に」: ✕「大阪で住んでいます」→ ○「大阪に住んでいます」. But 「大阪で働いています」 uses 「で」.
When 「ある」 means that an event or activity takes place, use 「で」: ✕「ホールにコンサートがあります」→ ○「ホールでコンサートがあります」.
Moving along or through a place takes 「を」; using 「で」 changes the meaning: 「道を歩く」 is walking along the road; 「道で遊ぶ」 is playing on the road.

etymology: 「で」 comes from the old case particle 「にて」 through a sound change (にて→んで→で), and spread from the end of the Heian period. 「にて」 itself marked place, means, cause and more, which is why modern 「で」 has all these uses.

similar.title: 〜に (place of existence)
similar.explanation: Both mark places and are the pair learners compare most: 「に」 marks where a person or thing exists (「公園に子供がいる」); 「で」 marks where an action happens (「公園で子供が遊んでいる」).

similar.title: 〜を (route / departure)
similar.explanation: Both relate to places: 「で」 marks an area where an action takes place; 「を」 marks a place you move through or along. 「川で泳ぐ」 is swimming in the river; 「川を泳いで渡る」 is swimming across it.

similar.title: 〜で (means / method)
similar.explanation: The same 「で」 (same origin, both from 「にて」). After a place noun it means “where”; after a tool, a means of transport or a language it means “with what”. You can tell them apart by the noun in front.

formation: 「で」 is generally thought to come from classical 「にて」: 「に」 (the point where something is) + the conjunctive particle 「て」, meaning “being in a place, (do something)”. So 「で」 marks the stage or setting where an action is carried out, not the end point the action reaches. Because it means “do something in a place”, it needs an action or event as the predicate. Pure existence (「いる」, or 「ある」 for objects) has no action, so it takes 「に」 instead of 「で」. The same “setting” can also be a tool, a method or a cause, which is why 「で」 also expresses means.

title: 〜で (means / method)
meaning: Comes after a noun and shows the means, tool, transportation or language used for an action: “by”, “with”, “in”.

senses.label: Transportation
senses.meaning: Shows what you travel by: “by bus”, “by train”. It comes before movement verbs like 「行く」, 「来る」 and 「帰る」.
senses.connection: Vehicle + で + 行く／来る／帰る
examples: I go to school by bus every day.
I came to the station by bicycle.
I'm going from Tokyo to Osaka by Shinkansen.

senses.label: Tool / method
senses.meaning: Shows the tool or method you use to do something: “with”, “by”. This includes chopsticks, pens, phones, email and so on.
senses.connection: Tool・method + で + 食べる／書く／切る／連絡する
examples: Japanese people eat rice with chopsticks.
Please write your name in pen.
I'll send the details by email.

senses.label: Language
senses.meaning: Shows which language you speak or write in: “in Japanese”, “in English”.
senses.connection: 日本語／英語／中国語 etc. + で + 話す／書く／言う
examples: Let's speak in Japanese.
How do you say this in Japanese?
I wrote a letter in English.

notes: Don't say 「足で」 for going on foot: ✕「足で行きます」→ ○「歩いて行きます」.
A vehicle with 「で」 is followed by 「行く」 or 「来る」, not 「乗る」: ✕「バスで乗ります」→ ○「バスに乗ります」 / ○「バスで行きます」.
「日本語で話す」 means “speak (about something) in Japanese”; 「日本語を話す」 means “speak Japanese (the language)”. The focus is different, so they aren't freely interchangeable.
Use 「で」 when the original material is still recognizable (「木で机を作る」) and 「から」 when it has been transformed beyond recognition (「牛乳からチーズを作る」).
In 「三人で行く」, 「で」 shows the number of people (three of us together), not a means. 「一人で」 means “alone”; don't read it as “using one person”.

daily.title: Asking how someone commutes
daily.description: Friends talking about how they get to school or work.
daily.example: How do you get to school?

daily.title: At a restaurant
daily.description: Asking the staff for a fork.
daily.example: Excuse me, may I eat this with a fork?

daily.title: Learning Japanese
daily.description: Asking a Japanese friend how to say something.
daily.example: How do you say “thank you” in Japanese?

work.title: Contacting a client
work.description: Telling a client how you'll get in touch.
work.example: We'll let you know the results by email.

work.title: Planning a business trip
work.description: Coworkers deciding how to travel.
work.example: Let's fly to Osaka.

etymology: This 「で」 has the same origin as 「で」 for place: both come from old 「にて」. 「にて」 could already mark means, method and material, as in 「舟にて渡る」 (cross by boat).

similar.title: 〜で (place of action)
similar.explanation: The same 「で」 (same origin, both from 「にて」). After a place noun it means “where”; after a tool, a means of transport or a language it means “with what”.

similar.title: 〜によって
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both can express a means or method, but 「によって」 belongs to written language and formal explanations and sounds formal: 「インターネットによって情報を集める」. In everyday speech, 「で」 is the usual choice.

similar.title: 〜ことで (means)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「で」 follows a noun (「電話で」); 「ことで」 follows a verb and turns a whole action into the means: 「毎日練習することで上手になる」.

formation: It shares its origin with the place 「で」; both are generally thought to come from classical 「にて」 (「に」 + 「て」), meaning “do something by relying on (a state)”. When the thing you rely on is a tool, a vehicle or a language, you get a means: 「ペンで書く」 = write using a pen; 「電車で行く」 = go by train. Since 「で」 only tells you “by what”, it must be followed by a real action (「書く」, 「行く」, 「話す」). With 「乗る」, the vehicle is the thing you get on, so it takes 「に」, not 「で」.

title: 〜へ (direction)
meaning: Comes after a place or direction noun and shows the direction or destination of movement: “to”, “toward”. Pronounced “e”.
connection: Place・direction noun + へ + movement verb

senses.label: Direction of movement
senses.meaning: Shows movement toward a direction or place: “go to”, “come toward”. It comes before movement verbs like 「行く」, 「来る」, 「帰る」 and 「向かう」. As a particle, 「へ」 is pronounced “e”.
senses.connection: Place + へ + 行く／来る／帰る／向かう
examples: I'm going to Osaka next week.
Let's head home early.
This way, please.

senses.label: 「〜への」 before a noun
senses.meaning: Adding 「の」 after 「へ」 lets it describe a noun: “a letter to ...”, “the way to ...”. 「に」 can't take 「の」 directly.
senses.connection: Noun + への + noun (手紙／プレゼント／道 etc.)
examples: This is a letter to my mother.
Please tell me the way to the station.

senses.label: Addressee of a letter or message
senses.meaning: Used at the start of a letter or message, like “To ...” or “Dear ...”. Also used in the welcome phrase 「ようこそ〜へ」.
senses.connection: Name／title + へ; ようこそ + place + へ
examples: Dear Mom, thank you for everything.
Welcome to Japan!

notes: The particle 「へ」 is pronounced “e”, not “he”, and it isn't written 「え」: ✕「学校え行きます」.
When the action is directed at a person, use 「に」, not 「へ」: ✕「友達へ会います」→ ○「友達に会います」.
To modify a noun, use 「への」; 「にの」 doesn't exist: ✕「母にの手紙」→ ○「母への手紙」.
Writing 「〇〇さんへ」 on a card or note to someone you know is fine. But in business emails and formal letters, the address line is usually just 「〇〇様」 without 「へ」; adding it sounds too casual.

daily.title: Planning a trip
daily.description: Friends talking about where to go on vacation.
daily.example: I want to go to Okinawa during summer vacation.

daily.title: Inviting a guest in
daily.description: A host shows a guest into the house.
daily.example: Please, come on in.

daily.example: Dear Yuki, happy birthday!

work.description: A staff member guides a guest to the meeting room.
work.example: Let me show you to the meeting room.

work.title: Explaining someone's schedule
work.description: Telling a coworker where the manager is going.
work.example: The department manager is on his way to the head office now.

etymology: 「へ」 was originally the noun 「辺（へ）」, meaning “edge, side, area”. It later became a particle of direction. Its sound changed from “he” to “e” through a sound shift after the Heian period (「ハ行転呼」), but the spelling 「へ」 remains.

similar.title: 〜に (destination / target)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning when marking a destination, and mostly interchangeable: 「駅に行く」, 「駅へ行く」. 「に」 focuses on the point of arrival and can also mark the person an action is directed at; 「へ」 focuses on the direction.

similar.title: 〜まで (end point)
similar.explanation: Both express where a movement goes and are often compared: 「駅へ行く」 means heading for the station; 「駅まで歩く」 stresses walking all the way to the station (the limit you reach).

similar.title: 〜への・〜での・〜からの (particle + の)
similar.explanation: Built by adding 「の」 to this use (same origin): 「へ」 can't modify a noun on its own, but with 「の」 it becomes 「への」, as in 「日本への旅行」 or 「先生への手紙」.

formation: 「へ」 was originally the noun 「辺（へ）」, meaning “the area around, the edge”. 「学校へ行く」 first meant something like “go toward the area of the school”, so 「へ」 focuses on the direction of movement rather than stressing arrival at an exact point the way 「に」 does. Because it expresses “facing toward something”, it naturally extends to “one's feelings directed toward someone”: 「母へ」 (to Mom). The pronunciation later changed from “he” to “e”, but the spelling 「へ」 was kept.

title: 〜と (and / with)
meaning: Joins two or more nouns (“and”), or marks the person you do something with, or do something mutually with (“with”).
connection: Noun + と + noun; noun (person) + と + verb

senses.label: Listing (and)
senses.meaning: Lists nouns one by one: “A and B”. 「と」 gives a complete list: these items and nothing else. It can only join nouns, not verbs or adjectives.
senses.connection: Noun + と + noun (+ と + noun)
examples: I bought bread and milk.
There are a book and a pen on the desk.
My family is my father, my mother and my younger sister.

senses.label: Doing something together
senses.meaning: Shows who you do something with: “with”. 「〜と一緒に」 (“together with”) is also common and makes the meaning clearer.
senses.connection: Person + と (一緒に) + verb
examples: Yesterday I saw a movie with a friend.
This weekend I'm traveling with my family.
I went shopping with my mother.

senses.label: Partner in a mutual action
senses.meaning: Marks the other person in an action that needs two sides: “marry”, “argue with”, “talk with”. These verbs can't take 「一緒に」.
senses.connection: Person + と + 結婚する／話す／会う／けんかする／相談する
examples: I'm getting married to my girlfriend next year.
Yesterday I talked with my teacher.
I had a fight with my younger brother.

notes: 「と」 can only link nouns. It can't link adjectives, verbs or clauses: ✕「安いと美味しい」→ ○「安くて美味しい」.
「と」 gives a complete list; to give just a few examples, use 「や」: 「パンと牛乳を買った」 (bought only these two things); 「パンや牛乳を買った」 (bought these and other things).
The partner in mutual actions like 「結婚する」 or 「けんかする」 takes 「と」, not 「を」: ✕「彼女を結婚します」→ ○「彼女と結婚します」.
When 「AとBと」 is followed by 「どちら」, it's a comparison, not a simple list: 「犬と猫とどちらが好きですか」.

daily.title: Weekend chat
daily.description: Friends talking about who they went out with.
daily.example: On Sunday I went shopping with my older sister.

daily.title: At a convenience store
daily.description: Telling the clerk what you want.
daily.example: A rice ball and a tea, please.

daily.description: Saying who's in your family.
daily.example: I have a father, a mother and an older brother.

work.title: Reporting to your boss
work.description: Telling your boss you discussed something with a client.
work.example: I talked it over with the client yesterday.

work.title: Preparing for a meeting
work.description: Checking what you need for a meeting.
work.example: Please get the documents and a computer ready.

etymology: 「と」 is a case particle found in the oldest Japanese. It could both join nouns and mark the partner in a shared action. Old Japanese often added 「と」 after every item, as in 「AとBと」; modern speech usually drops the last one.

similar.title: 〜や〜など
similar.explanation: Both list things with “and” and are close in meaning: 「と」 gives a complete list (only these); 「や」 gives a partial list (a few examples, there are others).

similar.title: 〜と同じ
similar.explanation: The same 「と」 (same origin), marking the other side of a comparison or pairing: 「AはBと同じです」. In this use, 「と」 marks the person you do something with; in 「と同じ」, it marks what you compare with.

similar.title: 〜に (destination / target)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning when the other party is a person: 「友達と会う」 stresses that both people arranged to meet; 「友達に会う」 can mean going to see someone one-sidedly or bumping into them.

formation: 「と」 is a case particle whose core meaning is “paired with ~”. Noun + と + noun pairs two things into a group and lists them completely (「パンと牛乳」). Noun + と + verb marks the person as your partner in the action (「友達と行く」). Actions that need another participant, like 「結婚する」 or 「けんかする」, also use 「と」 to mark that other party. Because the job of 「と」 is to pair with a noun, it can only link nouns, not adjectives or clauses.

title: 〜も (also)
meaning: Comes after a noun or particle and adds something of the same kind: “also, too”. 「AもBも」 means “both A and B”. After a number it means “as many as”.
connection: Noun + も; noun + particle (に・で・と etc.) + も

senses.label: Also / too
senses.meaning: Shows that something is the same as what was mentioned before: “... too”, “... also”. When you use 「も」, it replaces 「は」, 「が」 or 「を」.
senses.connection: Noun + も (replaces は／が／を); noun + に／で／と + も
examples: I'm a student too.
I'll take this one too, please.
I also went to Kyoto.

senses.label: Both A and B
senses.meaning: 「AもBも」 means both are true: “both A and B”. With a negative, it means “neither A nor B”.
senses.connection: Noun + も + noun + も
examples: Both my father and my mother are well.
I like both meat and fish.
Today both the rain and the wind are strong.

senses.label: Stressing a large amount
senses.meaning: After a number or amount, it shows the speaker feels it's a lot or a long time: “as many as”, “a whole ...”.
senses.connection: Number／amount + も
examples: I waited a whole hour at the station.
I ate three pieces of cake!

notes: 「は」, 「が」 and 「を」 can't be stacked with 「も」; replace them with 「も」: ✕「私はも」→ ○「私も」; ✕「パンをも食べた」→ ○「パンも食べた」.
「も」 assumes that “the same thing has already been mentioned”. If you say 「私も学生です」 when introducing yourself with no such context, people will think someone else was mentioned before.
A quantity + 「も」 stresses “that many”, with surprise or annoyance: saying 「三十分も待ちました」 to someone who's late sounds like a reproach. If you don't want to blame them, say 「三十分待ちました」.
“Question word + も + negative” is a total negation, and 「も」 doesn't mean “also” here: 「何も食べませんでした」 (didn't eat anything).

daily.title: Agreeing with a friend
daily.description: Your friend likes something, and so do you.
daily.example: I like that song too.

daily.title: Adding to an order
daily.description: Ordering one more thing at a shop.
daily.example: A coffee too, please.

daily.title: Complaining about waiting
daily.description: Telling a friend you waited a long time.
daily.example: I waited a whole thirty minutes, you know.

work.title: Checking who's attending
work.description: Asking if a coworker will also be at the meeting.
work.example: Is Mr. Suzuki attending the meeting too?

work.title: Describing the business
work.description: Telling a client where the company operates.
work.example: Our company has branches in both Tokyo and Osaka.

etymology: 「も」 is an old binding particle (「係助詞」). Its basic role is to add something of the same kind. The pattern 「AもBも」 goes back to old Japanese. The 「も」 in words like 「けれども」 and 「ども」 is the same particle.

similar.title: 〜は (topic)
similar.explanation: Both are binding particles that present the topic, and they're the pair most often compared: 「私は学生です」 is a plain statement; 「私も学生です」 means someone else is already a student and “I am too”.

similar.title: 〜question word + も〜ない (total negation)
similar.explanation: Built on this 「も」 (same origin): “question word + も + negative” is a total negation. 「何も食べない」 means “eat nothing”, not “also”.

similar.title: 〜と (and / with)
similar.explanation: Both can put two things together and are close in meaning: 「AとB」 is a simple list; 「AもBも」 stresses “both A and B”, often with some feeling.

formation: 「も」 is a binding particle whose core meaning is “add this item to others of the same kind already known”. So 「私も学生です」 assumes someone else is already a student, and “I” am added to them. It sits in the same slot as 「は」, 「が」 and 「を」, so it replaces them instead of stacking. In 「AもBも」, each item is added in turn, giving “both A and B”. After a quantity, it adds on top of the amount the speaker expected, producing a feeling of “as many as”. After a question word followed by a negative (「何も〜ない」), it means that whatever item you add, the answer is negative: a total negation.

title: 〜の (possession / modification)
meaning: Joins two nouns so the first describes the second: ownership, type, content and so on. Often like “'s” or “of” in English.

senses.label: Ownership / belonging
senses.meaning: Shows who something belongs to: “my”, “Tanaka's”, “the company's”.
senses.connection: Person・organization + の + noun
examples: This is my book.
Mr. Tanaka's car is white.
Please tell me the company's phone number.

senses.label: Type, content, origin
senses.meaning: Shows the kind, content, origin, material or time of the second noun. English often just puts the nouns side by side, but Japanese still needs 「の」: 「日本語の先生」 (Japanese teacher), 「日本の車」 (Japanese car).
senses.connection: Noun + の + noun (origin／content／material／time etc.)
examples: The Japanese teacher is very kind.
This is a Japanese car.
Where is yesterday's newspaper?

senses.label: Apposition / position
senses.meaning: Shows that both nouns are the same person or thing (apposition), or shows a position. Like “my friend Tanaka” or “on top of the desk”.
senses.connection: Noun + の + name; noun + の + 上／中／前 etc.
examples: Let me introduce my friend Tanaka.
The key is on the desk.

notes: In English two nouns can simply sit side by side (“Japanese teacher”, “city map”), but in Japanese a noun modifying a noun must take 「の」: ✕「私母」→ ○「私の母」.
Verbs and adjectives modify nouns directly, without 「の」. This is a very common mistake: ✕「食べるの物」→ ○「食べる物」; ✕「大きいの家」→ ○「大きい家」. な-adjectives use 「な」: 「静かな部屋」.
In 「AのB」, the main noun is B, the one at the end. Swap them and the meaning changes: 「日本語の先生」 is a teacher of Japanese; 「先生の日本語」 is the teacher's Japanese.
“A Chinese friend” isn't 「中国友達」; say 「中国人の友達」.

daily.title: Lost and found
daily.description: Asking in the classroom whose something is.
daily.example: Whose umbrella is this?

daily.title: Introducing family
daily.description: Showing a friend a photo of your family.
daily.example: This is my older brother.

daily.title: Buying souvenirs
daily.description: Asking where a product comes from.
daily.example: Where is this tea from?

work.title: Introducing yourself
work.description: Giving your company and department at a meeting.
work.example: I'm Yamada from the sales department at ABC Trading.

work.title: Exchanging business cards
work.description: Confirming contact details with a client.
work.example: This is my email address.

etymology: 「の」 is an attributive case particle from the oldest Japanese, used to link nouns. In old Japanese, 「が」 did the same job; this survives today in expressions like 「我が国」 and 「我が家」.

similar.title: 〜の (pronoun “one”)
similar.explanation: Comes from this use by dropping the main noun (same origin): in 「私の本」, a noun follows 「の」; in 「この本は私のです」, the noun is dropped and 「の」 itself stands for 「本」.

similar.title: 〜の (replacing が in a relative clause)
similar.explanation: The same 「の」 (same origin): in 「母の作った料理」, 「の」 works like the subject marker 「が」 (the dish Mom made) and doesn't show possession.

similar.title: 〜な + noun (na-adjectives before nouns)
similar.explanation: Both are used to modify nouns and are often compared: a noun modifying a noun uses 「の」 (「日本の車」); a な-adjective modifying a noun uses 「な」 (「きれいな車」).

formation: The pattern is “noun A + の + noun B”. 「の」 turns A into a modifier of B, meaning “the B that belongs to the area of A”, and the main noun is always B at the end. Whether the relation is possession (「私の本」), origin (「日本の車」), content (「日本語の本」) or position (「机の上」) depends on the meanings of the two nouns; 「の」 just links a noun to a noun. And precisely because 「の」 only works between nouns, verbs and adjectives attach directly to nouns without it.

title: 〜の (pronoun “one”)
meaning: 「の」 stands for a noun that was already mentioned or is clear to both speakers, to avoid repeating it. Like English “one” or “'s” (as in “mine”, “Tanaka's”).
connection: Noun + の; い-adjective + の; な-adjective + な + の; verb plain form + の

senses.label: Noun + の (“...'s”)
senses.meaning: In 「noun + の」, a known noun after it is left out. 「私の」 means “mine”, 「田中さんの」 means “Tanaka's”.
senses.connection: Noun + の (+ です／は／を etc.)
examples: This umbrella is mine.
Which one is Mr. Tanaka's?
This dictionary isn't the teacher's.

senses.label: Adjective + の (“the ... one”)
senses.meaning: 「adjective + の」 means “the one with this quality”: “the red one”, “the big one”, “a cheaper one”. Common when shopping or choosing.
senses.connection: い-adjective + の; な-adjective + な + の
examples: I'll take that red one, please.
Do you have a slightly cheaper one?
A quiet one would be good.

notes: Using 「の」 to refer to a person treats them like a thing and is impolite: ✕「あの背が高いのは誰ですか」→ ○「あの背が高い人は誰ですか」. For superiors or clients, use 「方」: 「あちらの方」.
The 「の」 after a noun already stands for a noun, so don't add another 「の」: ✕「これは私ののです」→ ○「これは私のです」.
With な-adjectives, add 「な」 before 「の」: ✕「静かの」→ ○「静かなの」.
The noun being replaced must be clear to both people. If you walk in and say 「赤いのをください」 without having mentioned anything, the shop clerk won't know what you want.

daily.title: Shopping for clothes
daily.description: Choosing a color at a clothing store.
daily.example: Do you have a white one?

daily.title: Finding your things
daily.description: Working out whose shoes are in the entryway.
daily.example: These shoes are my younger brother's.

daily.title: Ordering a drink
daily.description: Choosing a cup size at a café.
daily.example: A large one, please.

work.title: Checking meeting materials
work.description: Coworkers checking which document is the latest.
work.example: The new one is this one.

work.title: Borrowing things
work.description: Telling a coworker whose pen this is.
work.example: This pen is the manager's, you know.

etymology: Grammatically, this 「の」 is called a 「準体助詞」 (a particle that acts like a noun). It is generally thought to come from the attributive 「の」: when the noun after 「私の（本）」 is dropped, 「の」 takes over the role of the noun.

similar.title: 〜の (possession / modification)
similar.explanation: This use comes from it by dropping the noun (same origin): the possessive 「の」 is followed by a noun (「私の本」); the pronoun 「の」 isn't (「私のです」).

similar.title: 〜こと (nominalizer)
similar.explanation: Both can turn what comes before them into a noun and are often compared: 「読むのが好き」 and 「読むことが好き」 both work, but 「の」 can refer to a concrete thing (「赤いの」), while 「こと」 only refers to abstract matters.

similar.title: 〜んです・〜のです
similar.explanation: Generally thought to have developed from the same nominalizing 「の」 (same origin): in 「高いのです」, 「の」 adds an explanatory tone and doesn't stand for any noun; in 「高いのをください」, 「の」 stands for “the thing”.

formation: It comes from dropping the main noun in “noun + の + noun”: 「私の本」 → 「私の」. The dropped noun is filled in from context, and 「の」 takes over the noun's slot, so it can be followed directly by 「です」, 「が」, 「を」 and so on (「私のです」, 「赤いのをください」). After an adjective (「赤いの」), 「の」 works like an empty noun: “the ~ one”. Since 「の」 has no meaning of its own and depends entirely on context, it can only refer to things both people already know about.

title: 〜か (question)
meaning: Placed at the end of a sentence to make a question, like a spoken question mark. After 「です」 or 「ます」 it makes a polite question.
connection: Sentence (です／ます form) + か; in casual speech a rising tone is more common, though men also use 「〜か」

senses.label: Polite questions
senses.meaning: Follows 「です」 or 「ます」 to form a polite question. In writing, the sentence often ends with 「。」, though 「？」 is also fine. Say it with a rising tone.
senses.connection: 〜です／〜ます／〜ました／〜ません + か
examples: Are you a student?
Are you going to school tomorrow?
Where is the restroom?

senses.label: Casual questions
senses.meaning: Adding 「か」 to the plain form makes a casual question. It sounds direct and is mostly used by men. In everyday speech people usually skip 「か」 and just use a rising tone or 「の」: 「行く？」, 「行くの？」. Nouns and な-adjectives drop 「だ」: 「学生か？」.
senses.connection: Verb・い-adjective plain form + か; noun・な-adjective + か (drop 「だ」)
examples: Are you coming too?
Is it really that expensive?
You're going home already?

senses.label: 「そうですか」 for “I see”
senses.meaning: Said with a falling tone, 「そうですか」 or 「そうか」 isn't a question. It means “Oh, I see” or “Is that so”, accepting what the other person said.
senses.connection: そうですか／そうか (falling tone)
examples: A: Tomorrow is a day off. B: Oh, I see.
I see. Got it.

notes: When a question word is the subject, use 「が」, not 「は」: ✕「誰は来ましたか」→ ○「誰が来ましたか」.
Plain-form questions between friends usually drop 「か」 and use rising intonation: 「行く？」. 「行くか？」 sounds stiff and masculine, and can come across as rude to women or people you don't know well.
「そうですか」 with falling intonation means “I see”; with rising intonation it means “Really?” with some doubt. Change the intonation and the meaning changes.
Asking a superior or client directly what they “want” is rude: ✕「部長、コーヒーを飲みたいですか」→ ○「部長、コーヒーはいかがですか」.
In plain form, don't put 「だか」 after nouns and な-adjectives: ✕「学生だか」→ ○「学生か」.

etymology: 「か」 is an old particle. It could appear in the middle of a sentence (as a binding particle, 「係助詞」) or at the end to show a question or a rhetorical question. In modern Japanese it is mainly used as a sentence-final question particle.

similar.title: 〜か (or)
similar.explanation: The same 「か」 (same origin): at the end of a sentence it marks a question; between nouns, 「AかB」 offers a choice, “A or B”.

similar.title: 〜question word + か (indefinite)
similar.explanation: The same 「か」 (same origin): in 「何か」 and 「誰か」, 「か」 means “some~” and isn't asking anything: 「何か食べますか」 means “Would you like something to eat?”.

similar.title: 〜ね
similar.explanation: Both are sentence-ending particles and are often compared: 「〜ですか」 is a real question when you don't know the answer; 「〜ですね」 checks or seeks agreement when the speaker already has the answer in mind.

formation: The core meaning of 「か」 is “uncertain”. At the end of a sentence, it marks the whole sentence as “the speaker isn't sure and needs the listener to answer”, which makes it a question; after 「です」 or 「ます」, it's a polite question. The same “uncertainty” between nouns (「AかB」) means “not sure which of the two” = a choice; after a question word (「何か」) it means “not sure what” = something. So all the uses of 「か」 come from this core idea of uncertainty.

title: 〜か (or)
meaning: Placed between two nouns or options to show a choice of one: “A or B”.
connection: Noun + か + noun; verb plain form + か + verb plain form + か

senses.label: Choosing between nouns
senses.meaning: 「AかB」 means one of A and B: “A or B”. Often used to offer a choice or to show uncertainty.
senses.connection: Noun + か + noun
examples: Would you like coffee or tea?
Water or tea, please.
I'll go by train or bus.

senses.label: 「〜か〜か」
senses.meaning: 「AかBか」 puts 「か」 after both options and stresses “whether A or B”. It works with nouns and verbs, as in 「行くか行かないか」 (whether to go or not).
senses.connection: Noun + か + noun + か; verb plain form + か + verb negative form + か
examples: I don't know yet whether it's Monday or Tuesday.
Please decide quickly whether you're going or not.

notes: 「か」 means one of two, 「と」 means both: 「コーヒーと紅茶を買う」 is buying both; 「コーヒーか紅茶を買う」 is buying one of them.
「や」 doesn't mean “or”: ✕「月曜日や火曜日に来てください」 (sounds like “come on Monday, Tuesday and so on”) → ○「月曜日か火曜日に来てください」.
「か」 can also link verb clauses, followed by 「わからない」 or 「決める」: 「行くか行かないか決めてください」. Neither 「か」 can be left out.
The 「か」 in 「何か」 and 「誰か」 is indefinite (something, someone), not “or”.

etymology: This 「か」 has the same origin as the question 「か」. 「AかBか」 is generally thought to have started as two questions side by side, “Is it A? Is it B?”, and later became a way to express a choice.

similar.title: 〜か (question)
similar.explanation: The same 「か」 (same origin): at the end of a sentence it marks a question; between nouns it offers a choice.

similar.title: 〜と〜とどちらが
similar.explanation: Both are used to choose one of two and are close in meaning: 「AかB」 just gives the options; 「AとBとどちらが〜」 asks the listener to compare and choose: 「コーヒーと紅茶とどちらがいいですか」.

similar.title: 〜や〜など
similar.explanation: Both put several things together and are easily confused: 「AやB」 lists examples and can include all of them; 「AかB」 picks only one.

formation: It shares its origin with the question 「か」; the core meaning of both is “uncertain”. 「AかBか」 is generally thought to have started as two questions side by side, “Is it A? Is it B?”, which then came to mean “A or B”. So 「AかB」 naturally carries a sense of “not decided yet”, and often goes with words like 「わからない」, 「決める」 and 「迷う」. 「と」 has no such uncertainty: it means both are included.

meaning: Placed at the end of a sentence to seek agreement, or to confirm something both speakers know. It sounds friendly and soft, a bit like English “..., isn't it?” or “..., right?”.
connection: Sentence (plain form／です・ます form) + ね

senses.label: Seeking agreement
senses.meaning: The speaker assumes the listener feels the same and uses 「ね」 to invite agreement: “isn't it?”, “don't you think?”. Common when commenting on the weather, food and so on.
senses.connection: Adjective／noun + です + ね; い-adjective + ね
examples: Nice weather today, isn't it?
This cake is delicious, isn't it?
Your Japanese is really good.

senses.label: Confirming
senses.meaning: Checks whether something you know or guess is correct: “..., right?”. The tone rises slightly.
senses.connection: Sentence + ね (↗); 〜ですよね
examples: Tomorrow's meeting starts at ten, right?
You're Mr. Tanaka, aren't you?
This is your umbrella, right?

senses.label: Softening / gentle reminders
senses.meaning: At the end of reminders, promises or goodbyes, it makes the tone warm and soft.
senses.connection: 〜てね／〜ましょうね／じゃあ、また〜ね
examples: Get home safely, OK?
See you tomorrow, then.

notes: To tell someone new information they don't know, use 「よ」, not 「ね」: to say “Tomorrow's a day off, just so you know”, say 「明日は休みですよ」. 「明日は休みですね」 turns it into a check: “Tomorrow's a day off, right?”
Saying 「上手ですね」 or 「よくできましたね」 to a superior or someone older evaluates their ability. It sounds condescending and is quite rude; you can say 「勉強になりました」 instead.
Requests ending in 「ね」 like 「待っててね」 or 「お願いね」 are too casual for clients or superiors. Say 「お待ちください」 or 「よろしくお願いします」.
Adding 「ね」 to every sentence sounds childish or clingy. Use it in moderation in formal situations.

daily.example: The cherry blossoms are beautiful, aren't they?

etymology: 「ね」 is a sentence-final particle that spread in spoken Japanese from the Edo period on. It brings the speaker closer to the listener. One theory links it to the old particle 「な」, used for emotion and gentle urging.

similar.title: 〜よ
similar.explanation: Both are sentence-ending particles and are the pair most often compared: 「ね」 is for information both people share, seeking agreement or confirmation; 「よ」 is for information the listener doesn't know, with a tone of reminding or asserting. Together, 「よね」 means “That's what I think, and you think so too, right?”

similar.title: 〜なあ・〜な (exclamation)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both can express emotion, and some say they're related in origin. 「なあ」 is mostly an exclamation to yourself (「いいなあ」); 「ね」 is directed at the listener to share a feeling or confirm (「いいですね」).

similar.title: 〜でしょう (guess / confirmation)
similar.explanation: Both can be used to confirm and are close in meaning: 「〜でしょう？」 sounds more certain than 「ね」 and can come across as pushy toward a superior.

formation: 「ね」 is a single sentence-ending particle. It “hands the remark over to the listener”, inviting them to agree. So it can only be used for things the speaker assumes the listener also knows or will agree with: seeking agreement (「いい天気ですね」) or confirming (「明日ですね」). After a request, it turns the demand into “we're agreed, right?”, which softens the tone. Stretched to 「ねえ」, the “handing over” function gets stronger, so at the start of a sentence it becomes a way of calling for attention: “Hey”.
